d: Having a difficult and contrary disposition
ety: From crotchet + -y, using crotchet in the 16th-century sense of a whim or fancy.
s: He has a happy home life, two sitcoms on the go and a new book in the offing. So why is the comedian, actor and Observer columnist still so crotchety?

d: The name by which a geographical place is known
ety: Back-formation from toponymy. By surface analysis, topo + -nym.
s: ‘Tangerine’ is a toponym of Tangier.

d: A feeling of deep and bitter anger and ill-will
s: I could almost see the rancor in his eyes when he challenged me to a fight.

d: Earnest or urgent request
ety: From entreat + -y.
s: The entreaties of a lover and the rejection of the heroine lend charm to the stanza.

d: A clown or buffoon (after the Harlequin character in the commedia dell’arte)
ety: From earlier Harlicken, from Middle French Harlequin (in Italian Arlecchino, the name of a popular servant character in commedia dell'arte plays), from Old French Harlequin, Halequin, Herlequin, Hellequin, Hierlekin, Hellekin (a demon, malevolent spirit), probably of Germanic origin, connected to the Old English figure of *Herla Cyning (“King Herla”, a mythical figure identified with Woden) or pos
s: Motives are like harlequins—there is always a second dress beneath their first.

d: Excessively or hypocritically pious
ety: From Late Latin Pharisaicus + -al.
s: Thus Aurobindo Ghose stated that the puritanical, pharisaical British conquered in the name of liberty and usurped under the cloak of altruism.

d: Showing sustained enthusiastic action with unflagging vitality
ety: From Middle French, from Latin indēfatīgābilis (“untiring”), from in- (“not”) + dēfatīgō (“to tire out”).
s: He was respected by all who knew him for his integrity and indefatigable attention to public business.

d: A roofed arcade or gallery with open sides stretching along the front or side of a building; often at an upper level
ety: Borrowed from Italian loggia, from Old French loge, from Medieval Latin laubĭa, from Frankish *laubijā. Doublet of lobby and lodge.
s: Mr Carrados was standing in the loggia of the Hotel Beverley when a not unfamiliar sound claimed his attention.

d: Devoid of intelligence
ety: Learned borrowing from Latin vacuus (“empty, vacant”) + -ous.
s: The movie was criticized for its vacuous dialogue.

d: Hospital for persons with infectious diseases (especially leprosy)
ety: Borrowed from Italian lazzareto (archaic), lazzaretto, lazzeretto, from lazzaro (“leper”) + -etto (diminutive or meliorative suffix). Lazzaro is derived from Medieval Latin lazarus (“leper”), from Lazarus, from Ancient Greek Λᾱ́ζᾱρος (Lā́zāros), from Hebrew אֶלְעָזָר ('el'azár, literally “God has helped”), from אֵל ('él, “God; a deity, god”) + עָזַר ('azár, “to assist, help”). Lazarus is a Biblica
s: It is probable that from their inception the lazaretti did not house all plague victims. Wealthier victims were probably "quarantined" in their homes.

d: An unwholesome atmosphere
ety: First attested in 1665. From Ancient Greek μίασμα (míasma, “stain; pollution”).
s: It was into this lossy compression miasma that aptX was born.

d: A lodge consisting of a frame covered with matting or brush; used by nomadic American Indians in the southwestern United States
ety: Wickiup-like structures were built by many Native American peoples throughout the Southwestern United States, and terms similar to wickiup are present "among Native Americans in Arizona, New Mexico, Utah, Idaho, and California", but the source of the word appears to be Fox wîkiyâpi (“house”). Alternatively, it may be a variant of wikiwam (“wigwam”). Either way, its ultimate origin is the Proto-Alg
s: They say his real name is Cimarron Seven, of the Choctaw Indian family of Sevens; he was raised in a tepee; a wickiup had been his bedroom, a blanket his robe.

d: Marked by unjust severity or arbitrary behavior
ety: From Latin tyrannus (“tyrant”) + English -ous.
s: Yield up, O love, thy crown and hearted throne To tyrannous hate!

d: Noble and generous in spirit
ety: From Latin magnanimus, from magnus (“great”) + animus (“soul, mind”). Displaced native Old English miċelmōd (literally “big-minded”).
s: I felt vaguely he was a sneak, and remained quite unmollified by advances on his side, which, in a boy's barbarous fashion, unless it suited me to be magnanimous, I haughtily ignored.

d: Evincing the presence of a deity
ety: From Latin nūmen (“nod of the head; divine sway or will; divinity”) + -ous (suffix forming adjectives from nouns, denoting possession or presence of a quality). Nūmen is believed to derive either from Latin *nuō (“to nod”) or from Ancient Greek νοούμενον (nooúmenon, “influence perceptible by the mind but not the senses”) (ultimately from νόος (nóos, “mind; thought; purpose”)).
s: His interest in numinous objects led him on a quest for the Holy Grail.

d: Express criticism towards
ety: From Middle English upbreiden, from Old English upbreġdan, equivalent to up- + braid. Compare English umbraid (“to upbraid”), Icelandic bregða (“to draw, brandish, braid, deviate from, change, break off, upbraid”). See up, and braid (transitive).
s: Yet do not upbraid us our distress.

d: Disturbance usually in protest
ety: Possibly a rhyming reduplication of halloo (used as a greeting or to catch attention; used in hunting to urge on pursuers), hilloa, hullo (variants of “hello”), and similar words.
s: They made such a hullabaloo about the change that the authorities were forced to change it back.

d: An indirect (and usually malicious) implication
ety: From the Latin innuendō (“by nodding”), ablative singular form of innuendum (“a nodding”), gerund of innuō (“to give a nod”).
s: She made a devious innuendo about her opponent, who was embarrassed.

d: An awkward clash
ety: Borrowed from French contretemps.
s: The spat was just the latest in a series of contretemps between the RN and the AfD.

d: A tight sleeveless and collarless jacket (often made of leather) worn by men in former times
ety: First recorded in early 1500s. Possibly related to Dutch jurk (“dress”), itself of unknown origin and not attested before the 17th century. Derivation from Old French jo(u)rne (“day”) has been suggested.
s: A tall and very good-looking kid in a jerkin came out of the store and rode the coupé off around the corner and came back walking, his glistening black hair plastered with rain.

d: A small storeroom for storing foods or wines
ety: From Middle English buttry, equivalent to butter + -y. Piecewise doublet of butyric, butter ultimately being from Latin būtȳrum and -y being a doublet of -ic.
s: ‘This is the storehouse and buttery of my company of the Guard,’

d: Extremely pleasant in a gentle way
ety: From Middle English doucet, from Old French doucet, from dulz, dulce (“sweet, pleasant”) + diminutive -et, from Latin dulcis (“sweet, pleasant”). Cognate with Spanish dulce, French doux, Italian dolce, Portuguese doce, and Romanian dulce. Doublet of dolcetto and doucet.
s: Matthew "MattKC" Wong (actor) (2024), 6s from the start, in I ported THOUSANDS of apps to Windows 95: “Ah, yes, the dulcet tones of Windows 95.”

d: Payment or reward (as for service rendered)
ety: From Middle English recompense, borrowed from Old French recompense or Medieval Latin recompensa.
s: He offered money as recompense for the damage, but what the injured party wanted was an apology.

d: Someone who makes predictions of the future (usually on the basis of special knowledge)
ety: From Middle English sothsaier, zothziggere, by surface analysis, sooth (“truth”) + sayer.
s: The doomsday prophet / Whose words have all come true / The naysaying soothsayer / So cynical and blue

d: A sailing ship with 3 (or more) masts
ety: From Middle English barke (“boat”), borrowed from Middle French barque, itself borrowed from Italian barca or a Medieval Latin equivalent, from Late Latin barca, from Vulgar Latin barica, from Ancient Greek βᾶρις (bâris) 'Egyptian boat', from Coptic ⲃⲁⲁⲣⲉ (baare, “small boat”), from Demotic Egyptian br, from Egyptian bꜣjr (“transport ship, type of fish”), b-bA-A-y:r*Z1-P1. Doublet of bark, barge a
s: On being told, however, that the Norwegian barque Daphne was about to leave An-peng for Tamsui, I had my things taken on board, and we set sail a few hours later.

d: Suited to or suggestive of a grave or burial
ety: From Middle French funerail, from Latin funereus + -al.
s: Seven were chosen to push the funereal boat to the water, in honor of the seven faces of god.

d: A fringe region of partial shadow around an umbra
ety: From New Latin pēnumbra, from Latin paene (“almost”) + umbra (“shadow”).
s: The other places see the penumbra of the moon's shadow fall on the earth, so the eclipse is partial, and part of the sun's disc is still visible.

d: An ornament at the top of a spire or gable; usually a foliated fleur-de-lis
ety: From Late Middle English finial (“(adjective) final; (noun) ornament at the upper extremity of a pinnacle, spire, etc.”) [and other forms], a variant of final (“pertaining to the close or end of something, last, final”), from Old French final (“last, final; definitive”) (modern French final), from Latin fīnālis (“of or pertaining to the end of something, final; of or pertaining to boundaries”), fr
s: The steep slate roofs were topped with bronze finials so tall and fanciful they looked like drops of liquid sliding down a thread.

d: Misconduct in public office
ety: From French malversation, from malverser, from Latin male versari (“behave badly”). Compare Spanish malversación (“embezzlement”).
s: I see nothing quite conclusive in the art of temporal government, But violence, duplicity and frequent malversation.

d: Be earlier in time; go back further
ety: From ante- + date.
s: Actually, mathematical models of multi-sector growth models antedate the Harrod-Domar and Solow-Swan aggregate models.

d: Any armor for the head; usually ornate without a visor
ety: Borrowed from French casque. Doublet of casco and cask.
s: Helmeted Hornbill, Rhinoplax vigil (CR): Restricted to the Thai-Malay Peninsula, Sumatra and Borneo, this is the only hornbill species whose casque is solid keratin and therefore carvable.

d: Having or marked by a strong tendency especially a controversial one
ety: From tendency + -ious, after German tendenziös.
s: That he was a supporter of the cause was clear, because his reports from the front were tendentious.

d: Not sensible about practical matters; idealistic and unrealistic
ety: Derived from Spanish Quixote, the surname of Don Quixote, the title character in the novel by Miguel de Cervantes, + -ic.
s: Call it a brain freeze, another 'Aleppo moment,' or a mere campaign stumble, but Gary Johnson has stumbled again in his quixotic presidential campaign.

d: An upholstered armchair
ety: Unadapted borrowing from French fauteuil, from Germanic. Cognate with Old English fealdestōl (“folding-chair”). Doublet of faldistory, faldstool, and foldstool.
s: Gaston of Orleans was seated in a fauteuil, wrapped in a loose dressing-gown, everything about him betokening an indolent love of ease.

d: The ceremony of installing a new monarch
ety: From Middle French investiture, from Medieval Latin investītūra, from investīre (“to clothe”).
s: The Spanish constitution dictates that the king is obliged to dissolve the legislative body two months after the first failed investiture vote.

d: Beyond calculation or measure
ety: From Middle French inestimable, from Latin inaestimābilis, from in (“un-”, “not”) + aestimābilis (“estimable”). Equivalent to in- + estimable.
s: The Voyager spacecraft explored the solar system and continued into the inestimable space beyond.

d: Clear and bright
ety: From French limpide, from Latin limpidus.
s: The limpid glass doors reveal the living room clearly from the dining room.

d: A flaming torch (such as are used in processions at night)
ety: Borrowed from French flambeau.
s: Saint-Antoine has its cannon pointed (full of grapeshot); thrice applies the lit flambeau; which thrice refuses to catch,—the touchholes are so wetted....

d: A feeling facetious merriment
ety: From jocular + -ity.
s: Madouc was neither pleased nor impressed by Prince Bittern’s mannerisms, and remained pointedly unresponsive to his lame jocularities.

d: Footwear usually with wooden soles
ety: From Middle English patyn, patin, pateyn, from Old French patin, from patte (“paw, hoof”), from Latin patta, of imitative origin.
s: Nobody had appeared belonging to the house except a person in pattens, who had been poking at the child from below with a broom; I don't know with what object, and I don't think she did.
